answer: Within the NLSY79 1989 cohort (deduplicated n = 10,535, AGE restricted to 24–32), the probability that a respondent reports DISSAVED = 1 — i.e. withdrew more from savings than deposited — shows essentially no detectable association with AGE after controlling for INCOME and demographics: the INCOME-adjusted logistic-regression slope is β̂(AGE) = +0.0067 log-odds per year (p = 0.49), corresponding to a Q1(AGE 25) → Q4(AGE 31) predicted-probability gap of only +0.84 percentage points (29.24 % → 30.08 %) at median covariate values, with a bootstrap 95 % CI on β̂ of (−0.013, +0.025) that crosses zero. Without INCOME control the same model gives β̂ = +0.0156 and a +1.92 pp Q1→Q4 gap, so adjusting for INCOME absorbs roughly 57 % of the unconditional age association — consistent with partial mediation through rising income rather than a free-standing age effect. No nonlinearity is detectable inside the [24, 32] window (Box-Tidwell p = 0.43; 3-knot restricted-cubic-spline LR test p = 0.96; the predicted curve is essentially flat). Because the NLSY79 1989 cross-section spans only ages 24–32, neither a U-shaped life-cycle profile (the "rise then fall after ≈X years" pattern) nor any behaviour at ages outside [24, 32] is identifiable on these data and would require an older-age sample to evaluate; the apparent negative slope of −0.046 on the raw, un-deduped file was driven by 2,275 duplicate no-event rows that concentrated at slightly older ages. Interpreted through the saving-behaviour-as-proxy-for-temporal-preference lens (nls_bmi.domain_knowledge.1), this is a null, not a reversal: the early-career data simply do not speak to life-cycle preference change.

payload.workflow:
1. Load `data/nls_bmi_processed.csv` (12,686 rows × 9 columns); inspect types, missingness, AGE distribution, DISSAVED balance, basic correlations, quartile and income-tertile DISSAVED rates.
2. Diagnose near-duplicate rows on the full 9-column key; deduplicate to n=10,535 (dropping 2,275 rows in 124 full-key duplicate groups, 99% of which are DISSAVED=0 and concentrated at slightly older ages); verify that Pearson(AGE, DISSAVED) flips from −0.0411 (raw) to +0.0167 (deduped).
3. Fit four logistic-regression models on the deduplicated sample — M1: AGE only; M2: AGE + GENDER + BLACK + HISPANIC (no INCOME); M3: AGE + INCOME + log(INCOME) + GENDER + BLACK + HISPANIC; M4: M3 + a 3-knot restricted-cubic-spline on AGE at 26/28/30 — and record β̂(AGE), AUC, Brier, McFadden R², AIC per model.
4. Run nonlinearity diagnostics: Box-Tidwell test on AGE added to M2 (χ²=0.61, p=0.435) and likelihood-ratio test M3 vs M4 (χ²=0.002, p=0.964); both fail to reject linearity.
5. Compute predicted P(DISSAVED|AGE) at median covariate values on an AGE grid from 24.0 to 32.0 (step 0.5) under M2, M3 and M4, saving the curves to `predicted_curve.csv`.
6. Bootstrap (B=1000) the M3 design and β̂(AGE); produce 95% percentile CIs on the predicted curve and on β̂(AGE) itself (β̂ ∈ [−0.013, +0.025]).
7. Quantify the Q1(AGE 25)→Q4(AGE 31) effect-size in percentage points at median covariates: M2 +1.92 pp, M3 +0.84 pp, M4 +0.83 pp — documenting the ~57% attenuation upon INCOME adjustment (mediation).
8. Run a raw-data sensitivity check on the un-deduped file (M3 β̂=−0.046, p<1e-6) so the duplicate-driven illusion is reported transparently alongside the deduped primary result.
payload.artifact_descriptions:
main_nls.py — primary executed analysis: deduplication, logistic regressions M1–M4, RCS spline, Box-Tidwell, predicted-curve grid, B=1000 bootstrap, raw-vs-dedup sensitivity.
insp_nls.py — initial data inspection: shape, dtypes, missingness, AGE distribution and working-age bins, DISSAVED balance, Pearson correlations, quartile and income-tertile DISSAVED tables.
inv_dup.py — duplicate-row investigation: hash-fingerprint of duplicates, comparison of duplication status vs DISSAVED, sign-flip demonstration of Pearson(AGE, DISSAVED).
predicted_curve.csv — per-age predicted P(DISSAVED|AGE) on the 24.0–32.0 grid at median covariate values under M2, M3 and M4, with bootstrap 95% CIs for M3.
results.json — machine-readable summary of all coefficients, p-values, AUC/Brier/McFadden/AIC per model, bootstrap CI for β̂(AGE), Q1→Q4 percentage-point deltas, and the saved predicted-curve grid.
